Jensen agrees that 1080p, 8 GB of VRAM and four cores is all the Plebs will ever need.

text:
@GamersNexus you are probably not aware, that the 16gb of vram of the rtx 4060 ti make this GPU the BEST BUY for Iray rendering outhere! 

When rendering with software like DAZ3d Studio, if your 3D scene does not fit in your GPU VRAM, the rendering is switched to software rendering wich is obviously much slower. 

By the other hand the more expensive cards like 4080 does not add much to the Iray rendering speed according to varios users tests, not enogh for the price anyway. Notice that rendering speed is very diffrent for this use case scenarion. You don't need a specific FPS so any gain like 10-20% is not neccessary better because your are more interested in the PRICE per time spend to render. If you pay like 30% more only for a 15% time decrease (for example), that's a bad deal.

Please notice that 4070 is out of the question since it only have 12gb ram.

Also let me explain why the 16gb is the "sweet spot today". In IRay rendering with Daz3d the golden rule is to have at least the double ammount of VRAM as RAM and the other way around. Best buy RAM is 32gb or 64gb. Designers, when they design their scene try to stay in the common limits of today RAM (32Gb) because the more they will increase the RAM requirement for the scene, the harder will be for them to work with that scene. This makes the 16gb vram GPU the sweet spot/best buy of today (half of recomended maximum ammount of RAM for a scene). 

At this point one may ask: if the VRAM is so important, why not buying AMD? Well, many 3d rendering software i'm talking about does NOT support AMD. End of story.

So the smartest choice will be to buy a few RTX 4060 ti if you are into 3d rendering with software like DAZ3D studio instead of spending more money on a 4080/90 for not much  gain! This is how people like me ends up with buying a lot of those cards :)

 Nvidia know all this. That's why 4060ti was designed the way it is, for this 3d rendering market...

I hope this finally explain why this product was made and extra priced for. Unfortunatelly this is how they act. They increase the price for a speific need above production costs just because the demand exists. It's not fair but there is a Ferengi kind of logic behind this madness... :(

You may say that this is a corner case scenario. Well there are rendering farms outherhere with thouthant's of GPU. Just google rendering farm to see the industry i'm talking about. It's huge.

That's being said I will go and hit the buy button again for another Gtx 4060ti today for my rendering rigs.

text:
Hot take: 4060 Ti gives the same performance as the 3060 Ti using 75 to 100W less power.  It also does so with only PCI x8 lanes.   What does that do?  well, it frees up x8 lanes for expansion cards to mount two NVME M.2 using x4 lanes each. 

So what?  well... for old DirectX 11 machines looking for a DirectX 12 capable card (to play newer games or even upgrade to Windows 11) this fits the bill.  Even at PCI 2.0 tests show this card seems to take a minimal loss, and the lower power demands makes a decent mini-ATX power supply doable. 

Would a 4070 with x16 support be faster? sure.  Would that be noticeable for old rigs looking for some life that are CPU limited already? probably not... and those PCI lanes are like gold in old machines like my HP s5-1214.  It was a complete dog, over 10 years old, until I swapped in a Mini-PCI card to add SATA III, tossed the HDD for a cheap 1TB SATA III SSD, and added a Wi-Fi combo card to host an Intel BE200 Wi-Fi 7 and a NVME SSD slot (but only PCIe x1 lane).  Adding a USB 3.0 with Type A and C ports is easy enough for a PCI x1 slot as well. 

The limitation is obviously that the PCI x16 slot is only 2.0.  Ideally you'd think a x16 card would be ideal, even if it's a slower GPU... but testing showing this x8 card can hold its old against the older x16 gen cards, and do so with less power, means you can use a combo riser to mount this RTX 4060 at a full x8 lanes, and get those other 8 lanes for NVME slots (yes, they make such an adapter ;)).  

Suddenly that old Sandy Bridge machine with a legacy bios, MBR formatted SATA II HDDs, no graphics card and 802.11n and USB 2.0 is running 3 SATA SSD's, Wi-Fi 7, Bluetooth 5.3, USB 3 type A and C ports, two NVME SSDs at PCI 2.0x4 each... and a RTX 4060 with 2 HDMI or 2 Display port outputs.  Add in a TDM 2.0 module, convert the SSDs to GPT allowing activation of UEFI, and you have a Windows 11 capable, casual games, MS Office capable, web-surfing family desktop with dual monitors and 16GB of ram... FOR CHEAP-ish.

A cheap GPU like this that frees up 8 lanes AND IS EVEN AVAILABLE IN LOW PROFILE FORMAT is an amazing piece of technology IMO.

text:
why 8GB and 16GB.. From Nvidia:
Gamers often wonder why a graphics card has a certain amount of VRAM.

Current-generation GDDR6X and GDDR6 memory is supplied in densities of 8Gb (1GB of data) and 16Gb (2GB of data) per chip. Each memory chip can use either two separate 16-bit channels to connect to a single 32-bit memory controller, or two 8-bit channels, so two memory chips can connect to a single 32-bit memory controller. This allows a 128-bit GPU to support either 4 memory chips or 8 memory chips.

Higher capacity chips cost more to make, so a balance is required to optimize prices.

On our new 128-bit memory bus GeForce RTX 4060 Ti GPUs, the 8GB model uses four 16Gb GDDR6 memory chips, and the 16GB model uses eight 16Gb chips. Mixing densities isn’t possible, preventing the creation of a 12GB model, for example. That’s also why the GeForce RTX 4060 Ti has an option with more memory (16GB) than the GeForce RTX 4070 Ti and 4070, which have 192-bit memory interfaces and therefore 12GB of VRAM.

Our 60-class GPUs have been carefully crafted to deliver the optimum combination of performance, price, and power efficiency, which is why we chose a 128-bit memory interface.

In short, higher capacity GPUs of the same bus width always have double the memory.

​@Don1984-lc9rh McDonald's have the largest market share in the food industry, does that mean it is the best restaurant? NO! Most of the reasons why people buy NVIDIA are because of OEM's/prebuilts, people don't do research, NVIDIA is cheaper where they live or they had(notice the past tense) bad experience with AMD in the past(when they were dog shit).

And yes, NVIDIA does have better ray tracing, AI rendering and media editing. But most of those don't affect gaming. And if a $400 4060ti can't reliably get 60fps in games, ray tracing is useless unless you like slideshows. And DLSS 3.0 doesn't make it all up. Most games don't support it, and since the normal performance is so garbage, just get a AMD card, and turn on FSR 2.2, and it still will be competitive since the normal performance is just that bad. This is not counting FSR 3.0 which will be coming out soon™and should support older AMD cards™ and might support NVIDIA?™

And in the past, yes. AMD drivers were terrible. But AMD has fixed that. Most of the problems now are bad installs, lemons, weird configurations(something like old xeon's), etc. AMD drivers are on the level of NVIDIA especially on linux.

And you do pay for for NVIDIA. The 6700xt/6750xt with fine wine drivers which prices will go down soon when the rx 7700xt and 7800xt will come out, costs $320-350. NVIDIA does have some advantages. Like DLSS 3.0(when it works), and the better streaming, and for productivity. But most of that doesn't justify a massive increase in price, and most of that doesn't effect most people. I am pretty Angry with Nvidia. So I really dont like Defending it. 
But in this case. I have to Defend them. For a Simple Reason. 

The Standard 4060 is available at around 300 Euro. And the 4060 TI is about 400 Euro. 
And here is the thing. 
The 4060 is actually less Expensive than the 3060. And the 4060 TI costs the Same as the 3060 TI. 

So if its an Upgrade. Even if its a Minor Upgrade. It is an Improvement. Because it actually gives a Slightly Improved Performance for the Same Price. 
It also has a lower Power Consumption and allows for some New Software Improvements. 

So Overall. These Cards are Reasonable. And absolutely not a Waste of Sand. Because they Simply a little more efficient with no Drawbacks. 
And well. I mean dont get me wrong. 
But these Cards are for Gamers on a Budget. 
If I am a Gamer that Buys one of the Most Importand Parts of my Computer which is the Graphics Card for just 200-300 Euro. Then I am not the Type of Gamer that will Spend 200-300 Euro on a Monitor which allows me to Run Games in 4k. Heck just the 200 Euro for a 1440p Monitor is Likely asked too much. 
When I was on such Budgets before I got my current Job. My Monitors were usually supposed be less than 100 Euro. In many cases I just used Hand me Downs. 

The 4070 TI is a way bigger Problem. Because seriously. Its a 800 Euro Card. There is just no Excuse here. This is not a Card that should be Expected in a Budget Gaming PC.

text:
I work in the industry (not at nvidia, but downstream of them) and I want to kind of explain what's going on in the industry right now, and why these cards seem so underwhelming

during covid, there were mass retiring's and people moving jobs. You may have heard of the insane salaries in tech during that time. couple this with the war, and entire divisions getting shut down in russia and ukraine, and there was a MASSIVE loss of expertise in the industry. 

inflation is also really hitting hard. Companies are having to spend more to develop the same stuff, and shipping and supply chains are all fucked up. 

in the same vein, because of the recession, nobody is buying stuff, so the entire industry is kind of in shambles, and was preparing for a huge downturn cycle. The only reason this didn't happen, is because AI exploded, and hardware for AI is pretty much the only money maker right now, so Nvidia doesn't care about gamers right now, and they shouldn't. this new generation of cards is better for AI, and is more stable for those workloads, which was the point.

as expertise returns to the industry, and as new technologies come out, and as the recession ends, we will probably see a hardware renaissance. Nvidia doesn't hate gamers, a lot of the people working there are gamers. They just can't focus on you guys right now because you guys aren't buying anything anyways. Just wait this generation out, it's not for you anyways, and come back when the industry can start innovating again.

text:
That's the thing. You are right. Nvidia has NO competition. RDNA has tried and failed, it could have had the range of RDNA2, but AMD couldn't work up their engineers\testers or maybe couldn't get the production volume. So fighting Turing when Nvidia was still in RT beta - became impossible, though it was a nice try way back when.
RDNA2 had the insane advantage of TSMC 7nm, and remains to this day a power efficiency benchmark, whereas Ampere, like Turing, had to rely on engineering to manage Samsung's 8nm. And still the only remotely competitive card was 6800XT. And only because 3080 had a deadbeat 10GB frame buffer. And was pushing 350W. But AMD had(\has) no RT(realistically), no competitive encoder, no software, no features, FSR was barebone and, while in some cases, 6600XT did prove to be a few % ahead of 3060, ultimately that wasn't 5700 vs 2060 scenario, but a complete parity in every segment, but what good is a parity when your product is "number 2"?
And now Nvidia has the insane 4nm EUV node from TSMC, whereas AMD has to settle for old 6nm. And while both are day and night from 7-8nm era(4x the density), Nvidia's density is 40% higher than AMD's.

Which is why Nvidia can beat AMD's ~60bil transistors at 45bil. And with no power issues. Hell, it can shove up 76bil transistors, make them eat 450W and still cool it and run it stable.

AMD physically can not manufacture profitable and competitive chips, not even with MCM. I mean, if it could, it should've made 7600 start at TWO HUNDRED dollars. TWO HUNDRED. Not 250, not 270 - 200. 7900XTX should've been a 800$ 4070ti competitor while 7900XT would be a 600$ 4070 competitor. That would've pushed them SIGNIFICANTLY ahead of competition, would've forced Nvidia to do some Super damage control, but that's the thing - Nvidia WOULD afford a damage control. What is a practically at a loss manufacturing for AMD - is merely a margin cut for Nvidia.

AMD is dead. It's at its worst point since Polaris\Bulldozer, and while the architectural gap isn't as big, the manufacturing and efficiency gap is similar. But this time the worst isn't just the historical 1080ti, the king of rasterization, the worst is actually PLAYABLE RT. Which AMD can not pull off.

This is why AMD is rushing to rebrand their APUs for handheld consoles - it's trying to push its ultimate weapon - heterogeneous computing. But TOO LITTLE TOO LATE.
This should've been done YESTERDAY. Custom APUs throughout the mining crisis, instead of contemporary profits and even more lost gamer respect. Not some proprietary Steam Deck, but a universal chip. Because when you outsource R&D, you'll end up finding out that the outsourced producer would just R&D someone else's tech. Intel's. Or even Nvidia's, once it downscales Grace. Instead AMD is just riding the fabless existence and the freebies it can get from penny-pinching megacorps.

Just imagine that console-grade laptops were possible TEN years ago. Desktop APUs as powerful as ninth-gen consoles were possible TWO years ago. And by now AMD could've been on tablets if it actually owned the tech behind Steam Deck. Instead it just rebrands its barebone-powertuned laptop APUs for handheld consoles.

Intel owns it in CPU.... at 10nm. Vs 5nm EUV. Nvidia owns it in GPU, because it can afford newer fabrication.

So get used to such "generational improvements". I doubt that Intel can do much harm, or that Apple would try, let alone China. Unless AMD just pulls a titanic effort into finding a purpose for existing - the future of GPUs(and, potentially, later CPUs) is in jeopardy. Because for the first time in a while....

NVIDIA HAS NO COMPETITION.

There is something that no one mentions when talking about power consumption and thermals etc about this card.

Everyone says: "Well at least those are good" BUT is actually a horrible product even there. 
Why? 

Because this card has cut down cuda cores and raised the clocks to make up for the performance it was losing to 3060Ti from the lower cuda cores. 

So if this card had higher cuda cores like it usually happens with new generations then it wouldn't need higher clocks and it would have been even lower in thermals and power consumption while being better than the 3060Ti than it is now.
So it may seem good but actually the potential was much better. 
Nvidia is using the fact that TSMC builds better chips with less power consumption to raise clocks while lowering everything else so they can make profits by making cheapo chips with fewer cuda cores, less memory bandwidth etc.
The improvements aren't even from Nvidia but from TSMC over Samsung manufacturing. 


Lastly the 3060Ti is actually a better card if we consider that is built by Samsung.
Samsung manufacturing is inferior than TSMC both in performance and in power consumption. 
If TSMC built a 3060Ti chip it will be stronger and more power efficient. The 4060Ti is built by TSMC and yet is hardly better. Which shows that the architecture of the 4060Ti is basically inferior because a 3060Ti from TSMC will be better than what a 4060Ti is.

text:
The whole 1440p and 4k thing is for two types of people. One is a person with a huge screen relative to viewing distance where the added detail will show up. Everyone else is just lost in marketing campaigns, so they won't really get much benefit in their experience going from 1080p to 1440p or 4k. I feel like an entire group of usually smart people are getting fooled hardcore by a cabal of video card makers, monitor makers, and video game makers. Hell, I'll turn streaming down to 720p and not be able to see much difference.

And don't forget that, if you have a 1440p screen, there MUST be some ugliness when watching 1080p content. When going from 1080p to 4k, your screen is exactly 4x as big (twice as long in both directions). So if you want to display a 1080p source like Netflix, the algorithm is simple. Each 2x2 block of pixels renders the color of one of the pixels in the frame. Since 1440p is NOT an integer multiplier of 1080p, they have to use some kind of algorithm to decide where to add extra pixels, where to remove extra pixels, and how best to do that without messing up what you see. Never go 1440p if you watch 1080p content on the screen.

text:
I'll buy one.  I have a HP s5-1214 Slimline mini-ATX tower from 2018.  It only has DirectX 11, a SATA II HDD, USB 2.0 and 802.11n with integrated graphics that can do DVI-d or HDMI at 1080p.  It has a Sandy Bridge quad-core processor with 20-lanes of PCI 2.0.

This card, along with a few other updates, makes it functional again.

- I max'd the DDR3 ram to 16GB for $50.  
- Max'd the CPU to i7-2600K for $35.
- Added a mini-PCIe card to get two SATA III ports for $15 (limited to 4 Gbps due to PCIe 2.0x1 being 0.5 GB/s).
- Swapped the 750GB SATA II HDD for a 1TB SATA III SSD for $60 (plus $10 for a 3.5" to a dual 2.5" bay adaptor).
- Added an Intel BE200 Wi-Fi 7 with Bluetooth 5.3 ($35) using a M.2 slot combo card that also has a NVMe M.2 Type M slot (over the same PCIe x1 lane) for future use (also limited to 4 Gbps due to PCI 2.0x1 only being 0.5 GB/s) for $29.
- Added a powered USB 3.0 card with 2 Type A and one Type c ports (using with SATA power connector), and a USB 3.0 header for the front panel for $19.
- Replaced the HP 240W Flex ATX power supply for a 500W one with modular cables for $55.
- Added a PCIe x16 riser that provides two M.2 Type M NVMe slots with x4 each, and has a physical PCIe x16 top slot with x8 lanes for $23.
- I've been unable to find a 12-1 pin TPM 2.0 module for the LPC connector on HP/foxconn motherboards from that era, but I'm hoping it will appear in the UEFI after I change the SSD to GPT format and convert the bios from Legacy to UEFI.  If not, there are ways around the TPM 2.0 requirement for Windows 11. ;)

This gives me a casual gaming, Windows 11 compliant, DirectX 12 enabled, Wi-Fi- 7, Bluetooth 5.3, 16GB, NVMe SSD (PCI 2.0x4) system with 500W power and dual Display Ports for 4K video or 1080p gaming... and any connector I need for casual use... for $261... plus the card. 

A toss-away computer, became a screaming web surfer for cheap... and this card allows Windows 11 installation along with 4K displays.  

The fact that it only uses 160W makes it ideal for mini-ATX builds like mine, and the extra 8 lanes it frees up gives me dual NVMe x4 SSDs each at 2GB/s (vs even the SATA III SSD running at 500Mb/s over the PCIx1 lane).   Those lanes are like gold in a PCIe 2.0 motherboard.  Not only do you need lanes for data/SSD, but the processors back then only had a few lanes available (my Sandy Bridge processor can handle 20 lanes... 16 in that GPU slot, and 1 lane in each PCI x1 slot and the mini-PCIe slot). 

While it's possible to split and use PCIe x16 slots in x8x8 or x8x4x4 set ups, you simply CAN'T combine four x1 lanes back up to a single x4 if you wanted to run NVMe at full speed.  Without a x8 lane PCI GPU you'd either have to pick a x16 GPU or keep the integrated graphics and use that slot for say four x4 lanes of NVME. 

A real DirectX 12 GPU, with decent performance, dual monitors, and low power consumption is amazing IMO. 

If I was to forgo a NVMe x4 SSD and just stick with the SATA III SSD running through the mini-PCIe x1 lane (capped at 0.5Gbps) I "could" use a PCIe x16 GPU... but that also means a lot more cash for the RTX 4070, or an older gen GPU and more cash on a larger PSU, if you can find one in Flex ATX (600W is the largest I can find for this slim-tower design, and they've been out of stock for months, so a 500W will have to do).

text: @joelewing4216  There is truth to what you wrote. First, I was aware that Nvidia dropped the number of bits on the memory bus from 256 to 128, but not that they also cut the PCI-E lanes used in half. With only 8GB of VRam some games will run slower on a PCI-E 3.0 system. This has been proven by some YouTubers who tested the card on both systems. Most games run on a PCI-E 3.0 system ran with less than a 2% FPS reduction. There were some worst cases that were down almost 10%, but would not likely affect playability as the reduction did not seem to cause any visual stuttering or excessively low frame rates. Nevertheless, shame on Nvidia for making the 4060 Ti actually be such a poor performer. When I recently decided to upgrade from my ancient (10 year old) 1GB ATI graphics card I looked at both the 3060 Ti and 4060 Ti and decided on the 3060 Ti as it was $130 less and would run anything at 1080 and 1440P without issue. Both cards will run 4K, but at reduced quality. As my core i7 4771 intel based system has PCI-E 3.0, I am glad I made that decision. FYI, I bought an Asus TUF 3060 Ti for $320, new. The TUF 4060 Ti model was running $450 at the time. I am happy with my decision. I wanted to buy a new graphics card back in 2020, but I refused to be scalped by prices over MSRP.

text:
@joelewing4216  Nope, this is COMPLETELY and totally incorrect. PCIe 3.0 vs 4.0 has literally NO effect on a 3090 at x16, as tested by gamers nexus and others. At x8, this gpu should be totally under the available bandwidth. Gpus dont ever saturate PCIe 3.0, at least on x16.

I thought this PCI gpu bandwidth rumor stopped being a thing around 2017...
author: @jonnyj.

text:
@jonnyj.  I just watched a comparison video of the RTX 4060 on PCIe 4.0, PCIe 3.0, and PCI 2.0... all obviously at x8 lanes.  The difference between PCI 4 and 3 was almost nothing.  The difference between those and PCI 2.0 was barely real in all but the most extreme events.  literally 68 vs 74 fps ... 

The fact that this card can run even with a RTX 3060 using all 16 lanes, and do so at 75 to nearly 100 watts less power demand, means it's a perfect upgrade for old machines that you're trying to resurrect to DirectX 12, free up 8 lanes for two NVMe SSD's using x4 lanes each.  

Would a 4070 Ti with x16 lanes be better? Sure... if you weren't CPU limited to start with...  and if you wanted to spend $550 instead of $330... and have a power supply to power 200W instead of 160W.  

Everything about this card points STRONGLY towards older machines getting a boost of life.  Remember, Sandy Bridge only HAD 20 lanes possible, and some AMD offerings were even worse.  Modern machines don't have NEARLY the same limit of lanes as old machines, and a quiet slim tower that can do ok at 3D games isn't impossible now.

text:
What makes this all the more shocking is that the 4060ti has 2,310mhz and 2,535mhz boost clocks. The 3060ti FE is 1,665mhz base clock but averages around 1,900mhz. 

Now not to say that "it's not fair cos new card go BRRrrr", as that is the very nature of architecture. To get faster. But this shows that even with the clocks dialed up, the 4060ti can barely escape the 3060ti in raw performace. And here's why:

Nvidia is selling a 4050 as a 4060ti. 
4060ti is AD106, it's around 24% of the full GPU die (4350 CUDA cores) 
3060ti is GA104, it's 45% of the full GPU die (4864 CUDA cores) 
3050 is GA106, it's (you guessed it) 24% of the full GPU die (2560 CUDA cores) 

So in summary, Nvidia is selling you a card with LESS CUDA cores than a 3060ti, and it should be a 4050. Likely Nvidia felt jaded by the consumer backlash over the 4070 fiasco, so they just gave the consumers a even worse cut down card in retalliation, in the market sector where people don't want to buy the high end.

text: I think it's more that FPS is more important than resolution - once you've hit the point where the resolution is good enough. After that point overselling resolution was just for mugs - just like the people who pay $$ for netflix's 4k - from the distance most people sit from their TV you can't even tell the difference unless your wife is a hawk get the 720p option and save yourself money. The only thing resolution matters for is VR - when you strap the monitors to your face - then 1080p isn't enough. The resolution thing was a big thing when we were playing software rendered at 320x240 and then eventually got gpus that did 1024x768 - and up and up it went. But once it hit 1080p it was there. And by that time we're all using LEDs. The thing about LEDs is they only tended to look good at their native resolution. so unlike your CRT where you could have a fancy pants high res for your windows desktop and drop down to a playable frame rate for games you're better off having the monitor run at its native resolution. A nice 24" 1080p monitor does the job. If you need more screen space get a 2nd monitor. 4k is a waste of money. No more so than if you buy a big fuck off graphics card and it still can't run the game at 4k. You're much better off with a card that can push the game to 144+ fps with all the graphic options on at 1080p. VR is the only questionable thing here. If you use it for, say, something like assetto corsa and you hope to buy a headset in the future that has a resolution that makes VR look as good as a game running on a 1080p monitor viewed from a couple of feet away, well maybe you'll need a much better graphics card and more ram than this one. But fretting about its 4k performance for a monitor? Makes little or no sense.
author: @michael-3-l3

text: @michael-3-l3  I personally agree that for my own usecase I don't see any reason to go to 4K unless it's price competitive, I play at 3K ultrawide and for my viewing distance and monitor size that is the sweetspot. Going to regular 1080p hurts here, and the dropoff in performance for the 4060Ti starts already at regular 1440p which by all means should be the modern 2023 baseline that companies aim for at this price range. There are tons of affordable 1440p+ monitors available now, as many as there were 1080p monitors 5 years ago at similar prices too. The only reason it isn't the standard yet is because Nvidia and AMD are gatekeeping the required performance tier. And yes, there is a noticeable visual difference between 1080p and 1440p+ when you go beyond ..I'd say 24" screen size. Below that it's a toss and up to individual preference, but considering monitor prices are going against inflation, there is no reason not to desire the increased clarity of higher display resolutions. Not necessarily 4K, but higher than 1080 should be replacing 1080p at most screen sizes these days, just like 1080p did to 720p when +20" screens became the norm.

text:
Benchmarking the evil of NVIDIA:

To be fair on the price, the 1060 would cost $315.99 if it was released today, with substantially worse performance in every single category. If I offered you a $315.99 card and a $399.99 card and said "the cheaper one is a little bit cheaper but still in the same price class, it also will perform much worse in every single way you can use a GPU resulting in 50% to as little as 30% of the FPS and it will struggle to get to even 60 FPS in most games released in the last 3 years in high settings, with many titles made in the last 5 years clocking under 50 FPS." Which one would you actually pick? Double the performance for 26% more money or half to a third the performance for 21% savings?

I realize that inflation doesn't account for some of the price difference, as this card would have cost $316.45 in 2016 whereas the 1060 released at $250. But to completely put 100% of the blame on NVIDIA for a major shift in the market (33.23% increase in demand for parts used for gaming ONLY and far less supply of all the required parts and materials) is a little bit disingenuous. Inflation adjusted their profits on gaming GPUs have risen 21% in that time, but you actively compare things like the 4060TI and 1060 based on price despite the non-inflation adjusted price of 59.99% to make them sound 264.67% more evil than they actually are. They're only slightly evil, but again to be fair to them they have a legal obligation to their millions of shareholders which includes millions of ordinary people to do this. Their shares have risen 2045.87% in the same timeframe as the inflation adjusted price has increased by 26%. Considering a lot of people with retirement plans hold NVIDIA stock I would say that the evil they have done has been outmatched by the accident good they have done for ordinary people.

Nvidia this generation has basically been about pushing the consumer model stack one product number down compared to their historic norms, whilst also shrinking the die area of each chip model compared to last generation. The 128 bit bus is just an artifact of this.

This is also the reason for the 8 lane pcie bus IMHO.

Pure profit taking.

text:
Hi Steve, just wanted to point out some icing on this cake: the 4060ti is running on only 8 lanes of PCI-e. 
Nvidia uses the 2060 Super in their own marketing slides as a comparison. The 2060 Super came out in late 2019, while PCI-E Gen 4 boards didn't really come out until over a year later. 
This means that by their own comparison standards, a 2060 Super user could reasonably be expecting to upgrade to this card, but it's highly likely they do not have a Gen 4 motherboard. Derbauer covered some of the expected losses in x4 Gen 4 mode, and if that scales back to x8 Gen 3, you can essentially say goodbye to ~5% performance. That means that for anyone upgrading from a 2060 Super, it's quite likely they come out worse off than if they'd just got a 3060Ti instead.

You know what? We've been led by cash grabs for a while, yearly releases of hardware that may or not be relevant, both cpu and gpu. Many, many skews. Wtf. Is this our fault? YES. If there were no generational improvements but power efficiency for the same price, it would benefit everyone. You, me, she, he and the whole fukin planet.

One think i do agree, however. 1080p and 1440p need to go. 4K should be the norm with what we have right now on the mid range, and that goes back to game developers. text:
I feel like this isnt as bad as it seems here. They use less bus and get the same or slightly better performance, reduce power draw and get better thermals. Knowing that a lot of competitive gamers prefer 1080 for better fps, it makes sense to focus there and create what is a good foundation to use the improved efficiency on the next gen cards. Every company has to release products occasionally that arent necessarily a leap forward in raw power to set a foundation for more gains later.
Also, it makes sense to release your product as a good base, but generally not insane on its own to give partner companies a lot of room to work as well and create products that will sell very well for them, it makes them more likely to continue working with you and seeing it as a good partnership. 
That said, im not the most tech savvy, and dont know too much about this specific market as im relatively new to it, so im open to being wrong.

text:
This isn't even the first time NVIDIA has does this. Compare the Geforce GT 640 to the Geforce GTS 450 - the latter did much better on many workloads despite being a generation earlier. Why? The Geforce GTS 450 used GDDR5, whereas its successor used DDR3, with half the effective memory bandwidth.

NVIDIA seems to have missed the concept of 'working set'. If your have an effective working set size of 200MiB each frame, moving from 4 to 32MiB of cache drops your required DRAM bandwidth from 200MiB/s * fps to... 168MiB/s * fps.

I mean, this is effectively GPU architecture 101. Your working set is a) large and b) mostly trivially predictable, so go full-out bandwidth at the expense of latency and build everything as latency-tolerant as possible. Taking such an architecture and swapping in a component that reduces latency in situations where things are 'somewhat', but not trivially, predictable, at the expense of using a fair bit of power and die area, is an interesting choice.

This is also why it does 'better' on lower resolutions and with memory-bandwidth-cheap latency-or-compute-bound 'non-traditional' workloads (DLSS).

Nvidia acted horribly by making this card. 
What they did is cut down everything so they can create a very cheap chip that will give them higher profit margins. 

The 4000 series cards are built by TSMC that is has a better nm process than Samsung that built the 3000 series chips. TSMC can built the same exact chip as Samsung and it will be stronger with lower power consumption. 
If they built a 3060TI chip then that card will be better than all 3060Ti's out there in the market. 
So the fact that a 4060Ti built by TSMC can barely beat a 3060Ti show what Nvidia did. 

They took advantage of the fact that TSMC builds better chips with better thermals and they cut down the chip(less cuda cores than a 3060Ti). To make up for the performance of a worse chip than the 3060Ti they simply raised the clock speeds since they can afford to do because of how much better the thermals and power draw is when TSMC builds chips. 

If Nvidia actually bothered to create a better chip for the next generation by putting more cuda cores then this card will be barely 100W and with much much better performance. 
NVidia could built a 4060Ti that is easily 50% better than the 3060Ti with much better thermals and power draw but they chose to make a chip that was even worse and costs very low so they can make bigger profit margins from lower cards.

text: @wallacengineering8096  path tracing is the future of lighting in games whether you like it or not, sure not crucial right now and in the nearest future, but there will be more and more games in the future with this technology implemented. Why? Because using rasterization to generate shadows and occlusion for every light source in a scene with a lot of light sources would totally murder performance. Path tracing doesn't care about how many light sources there are in the scene, it calculates the same amount of paths every frame, so its performance ultimately scales better than standard rendering techniques. I think AMD will make cards with dedicated RT cores eventually. Intel cards have those too, AMD can't afford to be surpassed by Intel in new technologies department, even for marketing reasons.

text:
Everyone buying a GPU at this sort of price point today is likely to have a 1440p screen. Price points vaguely between $150 and $400, it'll last you hopefully upwards of 7 years, which might be longer than you're willing to keep that GPU.

But does it need to be native 1440p rendering? 1440p + DLSS Ultra Quality is potentially a thing someday; and DLSS Quality for 1440p target renders at ridiculous 960p, it's nothing, and it looks good.

4k in turn is not relevant for a $400 class GPU. Not at all.

Then of course it's the question of price and position in the lineup, which... well yeah.

But you're also getting something in return for a disadvantage at high internal render resolution - you do get a higher pure-compute (when not memory bound) throughput, allowing you to push per pixel cost and quality that much higher at reduced internal render resolutions. I am not convinced that i'm content with 8GB VRAM, but otherwise this is a compromise i might be willing to bet on, as i predict shader compute performance is likely to be increasingly a bottleneck in the future. So my prediction is, between 3060Ti and 4060Ti, in the future generation of games that are yet to come out in 2-3 years, 4060Ti should fare better and require less of a resolution and settings compromise, even though in today's games they are effectively equal. You're also getting better power efficiency, which is nice.

In a more competitive market, we'd be seeing a card marketed as 4060Ti come with 10GB VRAM as a base configuration, at the same price point, and it would have VRAM bandwidth advantage of 25% to the one that we ended up with, while the rest of the architectural decisions are carried over identically. VRAM capacity pressure would be relieved substantially as well, it would be so much better for barely any BOM cost increase. So GN's critique is absolutely sensible, but i wanted to highlight a different angle a little.

text:
@DBrealmadrid9606  This YouTube thread is probably not the best place to discuss. :) But generally I would say that PC gaming is qualitatively amazing (I own a PC and a PS5). With a PC you always have the option of paying less and lowering game settings, and I promise you that will still have a good time. 1080p gaming is still "high definition" and looks great. Unfortunately, though, 4K high-refresh-rate AAA gaming with no compromises is still very, very expensive. That said, the compromises have become far better in some cases. If a game supports DLSS or FSR (not all do) then the magical "4K 60 FPS" experience becomes attainable even with modest rigs.

My advice is not to compare metrics with the PS5, because the PC price tag will make you cry. Embrace PC gaming for what it is and find the best parts for your budget. Even if raw performance is less than what you hope for, it will still be fun. And, unlike the PS5, you can always upgrade the GPU in the future if your budget allows.

text:
Comparing to older generations the 40xx series all have the wrong names - the 4060ti is a 4050. In older generations the xx60ti has the same core than the xx70ti and a wider bus than xx60 or xx50's Versions. 
Just when you compare  the bandwidth of the 30xx series and the 40xx series. 
3050 128bit                    -> 4050 96bit 
3060 128bit                    -> 4060 128bit
3060ti-3070ti 256bit    -> 4060ti 128bit 3070(ti) 192 bit
3080-3090ti 384bit      -> 4080 256bit 4090 384bit

The only new cards that have a bandwidth comparable to the older gen are the 4060 and  the 4090. But another problem is the GPU cores. For example 3060ti and 3070(ti) had the same GPU core (GA104), but the 4060ti has the same GPU core the 4050 (notebook version) has (AD107) and if you follow Nvidia naming conventions the ones with 7 at the end were always xx50 GPU's, 6 at the end would be a xx60, 4 at the end would be a xx60ti (super) or a xx70, etc.
Sure Nvidia can name their GPU chips how they want, but this change is something that sounds fishy. I have the feeling it's a marketing strategy to sell low end cards for high prices. Like I said the 4060ti is in my opinion a 4050 and for that the price is a little high.

Regrettable there is a problem in some areas that you are stuck with Nvidia - I use a few professional programs that do not even offer an option to work with AMD GPU's and if they support it the the quality/speed is bad. One other example are the streaming features of Nvidia which you don't have with AMD.

text:
This is Nvidia's magnum opus of suck-itude. This launch is so horrible that even Intel's 11900K is cringing in disgust. The only things that could possibly rival this catastrophe are AMD's infamous Bulldozer architecture that held the entire company back for several years, Intel's aforementioned "Skylake on Skylake" stagnation, and Nvidia's own GTX 480 space heater. I would also say the 4060 Ti is a glorified and overpriced space heater but it doesn't even run hot enough to do that effectively. Calling it a "waste of sand" is an insult to every beach and desert on Earth. Now we know why Nvidia chose to not raise the MSRP of the 4060 Ti from the 3060 Ti, unlike every other GPU they have launched so far this generation. Who knew that any and all IPC and clockspeed improvements from the new architecture and TSMC 4N node would be completely canceled out by using a relatively tiny AD106 die instead of the 3060 Ti's GA104 die? Cutting the memory bandwidth in half by reducing the bus width to 128 bits? Who could have seen this disaster coming? But who cares, let's just put a bunch of useless L2 cache on there and heavily advertise DLSS 3 fake frames and ray tracing and call it a day... 

... Until you realize that DLSS 3 only really helps when you're CPU bound, but the 4060 Ti is crippled by it's 8GB VRAM and 128-bit bus so you are going to be GPU bound all the time anyways. It might have much better ray tracing on paper than AMD or Intel but the ray tracing and high quality textures use too much VRAM even at 1080p so the "RTX" and "DLSS 3" branding is all completely pointless. This GPU is a slightly overclocked 3060 Ti that has AV1 encoding... but the 3060 Ti also has NVENC so AV1 isn't that big of a deal. It's actually incredible that Nvidia managed to do this. They released a product that has literally *ZERO* (!!!) meaningful advantages over its predecessor that launched for the exact same price over two years ago. It either barely matches or sometimes runs *SLOWER* than the 3060 Ti in several scenarios, probably because that $400 GPU has double the bus width of the $400 GPU that's two years newer. Other than the 11900K this is the only case where it's accurate to say generational regression instead of progression (or stagnation). I guess you can argue that it will have longer driver support because it's a generation newer, but if it's already dead, cold, cremated, and ashes spread on arrival then it will struggle even more with games in the future. Actually, when you spread the ashes, you should do it in a sandy desert so the poor silicon can go back to where it belongs. That's how awful the 4060 Ti is.

I have a strong feeling that adding a few memory modules and increasing the price by $100 (GDDR6 doesn't cost nearly that much btw, it's just price gouging) won't save the 16GB version of this card. It will probably scale better at 1440p and 2160p but the 128-bit bus will still limit the GPU so much that the 16GB might not even be able to be fully utilized. Everybody knew that no amount of L2 cache could save the 4060 Ti but now we get to laugh at delusional Nvidia fanboys once again. Nvidia GPU launch day reviews are basically stand-up comedy skits at this point, and I love it. Thank you GN and other content creators, for providing us with great amounts of laughter to hide the pain. I'll be back for the RX 7600 and RTX 4060 reviews soon.

text:
@firatguven6592  People aren't buying a 4060ti tier card for productivity, tho. It's a tier of card relegated almost entirely to consumer class gaming. There are substantially better cards for productivity at affordable productivity prices for anybody seriously trying to do productivity. If you're doing it here and there, this card or any midrange card will be fine. If you're doing it professionally, you're buying high-mid to top tier consumer cards or even commercial grade cards. The 4060ti is kind of just bad. Even if you are doing productivity with it, the VRAM is a huge bottleneck. Productivity oriented cards usually have monstrous VRAM capacities and the ability to move it very, very quickly. This card has neither. So literally anything comparable for gaming will also more than suffice for your average productivity Joe, and anybody even slightly more professional will opt for pretty much anything faster. It's not even a consideration. 

As for the efficiency... it is a consideration for people with high energy costs, but ultimately, it would take a while to cost anything significant by saving 40 watts. You'd spend more needlessly upgrading. It would be the least of my concerns considering my other expenses. I could eat one less cheeseburger a month and make up for the energy cost. 😅

text:
@AFistfulOf4K  It's still overgimped. Memory bandwidth down, compute throughput up - didn't somebody come to think this makes for an unbalanced design which doesn't perform well, and costs in excess of what it ideally should? VRAM throughput isn't very expensive, cores sitting idle doing nothing waiting for VRAM is kind of expensive. Imagine 160 bit configuration, 10GB base, 25% more VRAM throughput, pressure massively relieved, easy 7% benefit over last gen, little more cost at the hardware level, easily same price point at retail if they were willing. We ended up with a bad design. Cutting down shaders would be a preferable way to bring the cost back in line, if so necessary.

You can't understand the complaint? You expect at the same cost, same tier, generation to generation improvement, not stagnation. When it's not coming, you expect people to be rightfully miffed. And yes sitting it out is an entirely adequate conclusion.

I'll open up another angle, that due to more compute throughput, at 960p to 1200p internal render resolution, which might be a good midrange target range, in titles that are yet to come in the next 3 years which may feature increased per-pixel compute load, 4060ti is likely to outperform 3060ti, which makes me view it a little more favourably than the video presents. But due to extreme bandwidth choke, there are going to be pathological cases as well where it performs incredibly badly, and you also don't really want a downgrade, since again we ended up with a bad unbalanced design.

Frame generation is very dubious benefit even in the best possible case. Increased latency. From experience with video processing technique, such as when DAIN is used to convert 30 to 60, and DAIN is really more advanced than what realtime algorithms can deliver, it's actually quite obvious. Looking at rapid hand choreography, i can see fingers flicker in and out of existence. It becomes better and less obvious at higher source framerates, but then, it becomes something which is unnecessary, since it was looking good to begin with! It's a solution without an underlying problem. Who cares about "number go up", purely for the sake of it?

We already had and dispensed with SLI since while it had that "number go up" framerate, it did not feel good to play. I have used a GTX295, internal SLI, and i'm not a fan. Split frame rendering hit or miss, alternating frame rendering looks "smooth" but plays just bad, plain bad.

text:
A modest amount of cache can compensate for lower bus width... at lower resolutions.
Cache hit rate gets lower as resolution increases, so its effectiveness decreases exponentially. 32MB cache roughly doubles effective bandwidth at 1080p (about 50% hit rate), but barely adds 25% more effective bandwidth at 4K (about 20% hit rate). AMD clearly showed this in their infinity cache hit rate graph last generation. You need 128MB to double effective bandwidth at 4K.

text:
I need someone to help me understand something. I feel like GN is incredibly biased with this review and I cannot fathom why when considering how much knowledge they have in this area. I wish I could have a discussion with them to understand their choices here but that's not really possible so here I am. I feel like a shill for saying it and its sad that this has come to a state where the deplorable actions that NVIDIA actually HAVE done, should diminish or skew the innovation that they are doing in graphical computing. I'll get stapled as a shill right away because of this comment and I honestly want someone to check my bias in my arguments if they find it cause I'm starting to feel like a conspiracy theorist at this point and I really want to figure out why. So, here comes a wall of text because I feel like I could literally write a paper about this topic and I want to get it off my chest:


Currently, the 6700 XT sits at like ~$330 today (originally priced at $479) and had worse performance in most cases (not all), though not by much, than the 4060 ti 8GB on all games and even had better performance in some games. The 4060 ti 8GB is to be released at $399 at launch which is around a 20% increase in price from the 6700 XT. So obviously, we don't seem to get 20% more performance. But price to performance does not scale on a linear scale by any means and has never done that so I don't feel like this is a valid argument at all. One could say that its quite sad that it isn't more though, which I agree with to a certain extent, but that takes me to the next argument: 

The biggest thing here, which I CANNOT fully wrap my head around, is how all of these test are done without DLSS? And on top of that, its done without DLSS 3!? Now, they bring up at 30:00 that DLSS is not a justifiable reason to differentiate the card from its competitors, which I don't understand how someone with this much knowledge can even say. You buy an NVIDIA card BECAUSE of the technology that have developed with their insane engineers, which other competitors like AMD simply do not have any comparable alternative to. In fact, you buy ANY card because of its technology, which resided way more heavily in architecture improvements of the card and things like transistor count or memory efficiency. STILL new cards gave value because they introduced other NEW features compared to their competitors.

Doing a review without DLSS is literally like removing parts/features of your new card and then comparing it to the competition. There have been so many technological advancements in hardware for graphical computing throughout their whole history and you choose to ignore that? Because of what? What possible reasons would say that this would be a fair test? 

This is like avoiding putting a GPU into the 16x PCIe lane when that was first supported. Its like making sure to use an old driver to not test a card's capability of using compute shaders when that was first implemented. Its like arguing that multi-threading as a whole was useless because some programs behaved weird when Intel first introduced it, which might even be an even MORE valid argument than ignoring DLSS as this actually could cause some programs to be unusable. Yes these are not EXACTLY comparable but honestly are good analogies in my opinion. You are removing a CORE architectural feature of the hardware that has been deliberately put there and then complaining about its performance.

Are we that one dimensional that we only focus on transistor count or memory usage like there are not a huge array of details in the hardware that makes it what it is? These are incredibly important for GPU performance but DLSS is legit the technology that aliviates these issues for the graphics card. You are rendering at lower resolutions, which reduces VRAM usage of all resources that are resolution-dependent as they scale down, and upon that you are generating new frames with DLSS 3.0 to give huge performance gains in higher resolutions like 4k. 

THAT is what you are paying extra for. THAT is what is contributing to a graphical computing revolution. Its a NEW way of handling performance, which before was up to increasing transistor count but is not something that scales the same any more. Just like introducing multi core processors was a NEW way of unlocking huge performance boosts. Its not just scaling up current solutions, its a completely different way to handle the problem. 

DLSS is not perfect though and that IS something to consider. But saying that its BAD or UNPLAYABLE is an absolute CRAZY stretch. In 99% of cases it gives huge benefits for graphical fidelity as you can bump up your graphical settings, and in that 1% you WILL notice some weird frame generation, which is a valid critique. However, this is a technology that is always improving and has been proven too just in a couple of years. 

There is so much to critique NVIDIA on and people choose to shit on the cards whilst absolutely ignoring the insane technology that has been in these cards for 3 years now. Every game that comes out nowadays, that actually benefit from it, has DLSS available, so that's not really an argument either. The argument that GN presents for not including DLSSS here is legit a non-sequitur by definition: it's an argument whose logic is not related to the conclusion that is made. 

Nvidia DID show DLSS 3 results compared to DLSS 2, which in GNs opinion was misleading. Now even IF we agree that it was misleading: how does the logic then follow to not include the technology in any of your benchmarks and deem it "a waste of sand"? How is this the logical conclusion? The logical conclusion would be that NVIDIAs marketing team shows the numbers that are the best to show the capabilities of the new card which SHOULD be deemed biased and is the whole reasons why channels like this are SO important for the consumers. The conclusion should however not be: "... therefore the technology is useless and does not give any real value to the product". Their real argument seems to lie in the fact that they just don't think that DLSS is something that is good enough to counteract the disappointing increases in regular rendering. The exact reason for that is what I don't understand.

In 5 years time. Every single GPU will have AI upscaling of assets, post processing, and resolution. This is something that I don't doubt for a second. Its an inevitable future and I guarantee that every review of those graphics cards will put those numbers FIRST as it will be something that is so normalized that its not even worth mentioning anymore. Its a core way of how graphics development will look like in the future and ignoring it now, for no good reason, seems so incredibly strange to me and honestly feels more that its an issue of logistics on how to accurately compare these technologies when the competition does not have it. This however, is not a sufficient reason to exclude this data and not show ANY of it.

text:
​ @Tucanazo69  there is stuff like OneAPI Level Zero for Intel (and it is portable/cross-platform in theory, as it has "backends" allowing it to run on all three manufacturers' hardware) and ROCm (which uses HIP which is pretty similar to CUDA and also is portable natively for all three platforms, even to OneAPI LZ). 
Even though they exist and don't have much problems (at least which I'm aware of), the problem is that AMD and Intel are not flooding the problem with sponsorship money for implementations of every program using these compute APIs.
The consumers themselves are already neck-deep into that monopoly so there's no reason to buy non-NVIDIA hardware so there's no reason to make changes to the software stack to support anything else.
This can be moved by the competition having hardware with impressive "productivity" performance available for cheap and having any software support (through development sponsorship/developing it themselves). 
AMD and Intel already know this, of course :). ROCm and oneAPI are seeing much more development and support expansion lately. For example, Intel's OneAPI DPC++ aims to support compiling both HIP and LZ code for any hardware.

The thing is: 20 years ago, high tier cards were targeted at 720p, 18 years ago they were targeted at 900p, 15 years ago they were targeted at 1080p. Now, if we jump to 2016 or so, upper-mid tier cards were being targeted at 1440p (GTX 1070), same with the next gen (RTX 2060/2070, RX 5700 XT), and then the next generation they started marketing them at 1080p again.

So... we are paying more now for cards that apparently can't properly handle resolutions that were mainstream for previous generations. And yes, I understand games are more demanding now. But guess what, they are more demanding precisely because hardware apparently would be more powerful. Graphics stagnated for a long time as they were still running games targeted at PS4 and Xbox One.

On another note: C'mon, 8GB of VRAM? 100USD more for 8GB more? One of their alleged reasons for increasing prices on GPUs was that memory was getting more expensive. Right now memory is the cheapest it has been for years and they increase 100USD for 8GB more of memory.

@termitreter6545  So for context, I'm not playing a lot of modern AAA titles because I'm still playing catch up (the backlog never gets any smaller ya know), so the only brand new titles I tend to play are Indies that I can buy for 10 bucks and run on a toaster. Other than that, I play FFXIV and Overwatch, neither of which are especially demanding on the gpu. So 1440p works for me on all of those. 

That said, my original point was that the 1060 was marketed as a 1080p card, 2060 and 2060 super were both 1080p/1440p cards according to marketing (grain of salt here, we all know that marketing is rarely accurate). The 3060Ti was marketed as a 1440p card (which it CAN do depending on what titles you're playing and what settings you're cool with, lots of games still look great on medium to high settings these days). 

The 4060Ti being marketed as a 1080p card, providing almost no performance uplift over the previous gen, all for the same price, without providing additional VRAM for longevity, is an embarrasment, and should be treated as such. The 3060Ti was a solid improvement over the 2060 Super, which was a modest improvement over a 1060. The 4060Ti shouldn't have had an 8GB variant, it should just be the 16GB at 400, and it should have kept the same memory bus so that wasn't bottlenecking it. But that would have meant Jensen could only afford infinity leather jackets instead of infinity plus 2, so here we are. 

PC gaming hardware has been pretty sad lately, but the brightside seems to be that a lot of this stuff isn't selling that well, so good job everyone! Keep that energy up and maybe we'll force AMD and Nvidia to get their heads out of their asses and actually start competing again.

So if you don't care about the fancy lighting that is going to TANK your performance to the point the fancy monitor you bought to play games on may not even be able to be used to it's full potential, then just stick with the 1080 Ti or go pick one up used. If you do really care that much about raytracing that you are willing to play games on your 125hz+ monitor at 40-80fps just to have some fancy lighting save a tad more money and get yourself a 3070 Ti or 4070.

text:
Don't you guys see what's happening?  Software rendering technologies (RT, UE5's features, etc) are out-growing raw hardware performance.  This shouldn't be a surprise to anyone.  We're in the middle of a buffer state with current tech.  It's going to be a few years before the hardware catches up to the software.  DLSS and AI in general are just the first steps towards that.

I don't think this video is fair to the current state that the industry is in.  Sure, marketing with these big companies is always bad, but to their credit, they heavily marketed DLSS.  

Why did you only compare DLSS in Cyberpunk (at 1080p)???  You should know that the higher the resolution, the more relative gain you get from DLSS.  But you ran it at 1080???  You say DLSS 3 is not sufficient to justify buying the card, but you only show one game at a resolution where its benefit is the least... ???

They can only make marginal gains in raw performance, but they can make massive gains in DLSS and AI.  Nvidia knows this and I think they're making the long term investment of improving DLSS and AI - compared to AMD, who is making the short term investment just to catch up.  AMD is struggling with RT and upscaling.  It's clear their efforts are spent on rasterization and raw performance.  Well, Nvidia thinks that is not the future... and I agree.

The deal used to be, your GPU loses value, but you get to upgrade by paying the difference.
Now if you want twice the performance, you pay twice the money, AND your old GPU loses most of its value too.
That's the power of monopoly and greed. Upgrading is becoming unsustainable unless you're very rich.

text:
​​ @somberz  4070 Ti is... Acceptable, mostly. It's main issue is it's price combined with its 12 GB of VRAM. It's VRAM will start to be a bottleneck in fairly short order I believe. For the 4070 it's still an issue but somewhat less of an issue because there's less hardware in the rest of the card to be bottlenecked, but even then really it should have 16GB, or atleast 14GB, and the 4070Ti really should have 18GB, or atleast 16GB. 

So far as the 40 series goes, the 4070 Ti is one of the better ones, behind the 4090, and slightly worse than the 4070, price to (time averaged over the next 4 years, estimated) performance wise.

Given all this, whether it was a mistake or not depends on your circumstance. I bought a 4070, if I had a 2080 Super or better beforehand, I'd say this would have been a mistake, but I had a 2070 and by buying a 4070 I could mid-life upgrade, and so leverage value from the rest of the system that way. 

Ultimately, the 40 series in general is fairly poor value, but it can under some circumstances still be worth it, and only you can determine if it is worth it or not. Overall, given what's on offer, for a new build mid range PC, I'd say it was the second best option and only just barely worse than the best option of the 4070.

text:
I hate to be the guy to correct a legend such as Steve but... the reason the performance is tanking at 4K is because of its raster pipeline (ROPs), and NOT the bus width. The pixel throughput of the 4060Ti and 3060Ti is actually surprisingly close (121.7 vs. 133.2 GPixels/s). These are the numbers I've taken from TPU so the actual throughput may vary based on actual frequencies. And the reason for this is 3060Ti's 80x raster pipeline versus 4060Ti's 48x. But since the N5 has an enormous clock speed advantage over Samsung's 8nm, the difference is nullified to quite an extent. 
And that's why in ROP bound scenarios, the 4060Ti is basically performing on par with the 3060Ti. 
As for the bus width and on-board L2 cache, RDNA2 has proved that you can indeed make-up for the lack of raw bandwidth with lower latencies but of course it's not a substitute. It merely reduces the GPU's dependency on memory controllers.

text:
It makes sense that it performs terribly as the resolution increases. It is not that using cache is flawed but that 32MB is way too little. At 4K a single frame buffer at 32bpp is 33.75MB.  For the cache to be really effective it should contain 2 copies of a frame buffer at 64 or even 128bpp if hdr is going to be used, a z buffer, and some extra for whatever the shaders will be doing. So for 4K you would want something like 128MB.
A 1080p framebuffer is 7.9MB so you can fit two copies, a zbuffer and have some to spare for the shaders. Then all the repeated access within a frame can be cached and the shaders will not have to wait for vram access more than once for the things in cache. 
As usual it is Nvidia choosing to give way to little for the price.
